strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision application: generating anatomically detailed reports from 3D CT. Combining global slice information, region-specific features, and quantitative attributes is clinically motivated and forms a coherent framework.

R2 pooling provides a simple, economical adaptation of slow–fast tokenization: selecting representative slices using anatomical masks reduces the visual sequence from D×T to D+T tokens while retaining denser features on selected slices.

On the official RadGenome-Chest CT split, the complete model improves CA-F1 from M3D’s 0.435 to 0.450 and the GPT-based score from 47.243 to 48.837. Component ablations support complementary contributions from mask features and attribute prompts to these metrics.

The manuscript acknowledges relevant foundations, including LITA, MAIRA-SEG/Osprey, SAT, and RadGPT. The supplement supplies useful training settings, an attribute prompt template, and extraction pseudocode.
weaknesses: The quantitative attribute pipeline has a substantive correctness concern. Supplementary Fig. 4 computes organ volume by summing mask voxels and lesion diameter from bounding-box extents in voxel indices, whereas Fig. 5 labels these quantities in ml and mm. No voxel-spacing conversion or physical-coordinate calculation is shown. As documented, these are not valid physical measurements across scans with different spacing; the bounding-box extent is also only a diameter proxy. This directly undermines the claimed clinical meaning of a central component.

The comparisons do not adequately establish advancement over the closest approaches. Reg2RG and MS-VLM are discussed but not evaluated, although they directly address region-guided CT reporting and slice-based aggregation. Furthermore, the 48-hour training cap leaves CT2Rep explicitly undertrained. The supplement claims a common LLaMA3-8B decoder for all baselines, while the main text states that CT2Rep did not use an LLM. These issues limit the fairness and interpretability of the state-of-the-art claim.

The clinical superiority claims exceed the mixed evidence. The proposed model’s GREEN score is 0.278, below both M3D’s 0.297 and CT2Rep’s 0.374, and its ROUGE-L and METEOR also trail M3D. The explanation that CT2Rep’s GREEN result is biased by normal-case overfitting is not supported by a stratified analysis. There are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or clinician evaluations to establish the reliability and clinical significance of the modest gains on the preferred metrics.

The experiments do not sufficiently test the specific promise of comprehensive regional reporting. Aggregate F1 over 18 abnormalities and a single qualitative lung example do not establish anatomical localization, measurement accuracy, or performance across all six regions. There is also no analysis of segmentation errors or missing masks, despite masks driving slice selection, regional features, and attribute prompts simultaneously. External validation would further strengthen the broad applicability claims.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, originality is primarily in integration: mask-aware extraction is adapted from MAIRA-SEG, attribute prompting follows existing work, and R2 replaces uniform slow-token sampling with maximum-mask-area selection. This combination could be valuable, but its distinctive benefit remains insufficiently isolated. R2 versus LITA produces mixed metric changes, and the study lacks controls separating structured regional supervision and extra segmentation-derived information from the proposed architectural choices.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete. The six-region mapping, precise pooling configuration, lesion-mask acquisition, handling of absent masks, and baseline training protocols need clearer specification. The abstract claims public code without providing a repository link in the supplied manuscript. Token reduction is established analytically, but end-to-end latency and memory—including segmentation and regional report generation—are not measured. Reporting errors, including the Table 1 reference to MS-VLM and the claim that the complete model leads all ablations despite contrary entries, also require correction.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision application: generating detailed reports from volumetric CT. Combining global slice coverage, region-specific features, and quantitative anatomical information is a clinically motivated design.

R2 pooling offers a simple, economical adaptation of slow–fast tokenization: representative slices are selected using anatomical masks, reducing the vision-token count from D×T to D+T. The integration with segmentation tokens and textual attributes is coherent.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence on the official RadGenome-Chest CT split. The complete model improves CA-F1 from M3D’s 0.435 to 0.450 and the GPT-based score from 47.243 to 48.837. Component ablations support the usefulness of both mask features and attributes for these metrics.

The manuscript acknowledges the methods underlying its components, including LITA, MAIRA-SEG/Osprey, SAT, and RadGPT. The supplement supplies useful training settings, attribute-extraction pseudocode, and a prompt template.
weaknesses: The quantitative attribute extraction has a substantive correctness problem as documented. Supplementary Fig. 4 computes volume by summing mask voxels and diameter as the largest bounding-box extent in voxel coordinates, whereas Fig. 5 labels these quantities as milliliters and millimeters. No voxel-spacing conversion or physical-coordinate resampling is specified. Bounding-box extent also requires justification as a lesion-diameter estimate. Because these measurements directly condition the generated reports, this is more consequential than a presentation error.

The comparisons do not establish the claimed advance over closely related approaches. Reg2RG, explicitly discussed as combining regional segmentation features with global CT features, is absent from the experiments; MS-VLM is also discussed but not evaluated. Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the incremental adaptations of existing pooling, mask encoding, and attribute prompting require stronger comparisons to establish their significance.

Baseline training introduces important uncertainty. The supplement imposes a 48-hour budget on two A100 GPUs, and Section 4.2 explicitly acknowledges that CT2Rep was insufficiently trained. The supplement also says all comparison methods use LLaMA3-8B, while Section 4.2 states that CT2Rep could not incorporate an LLM. Convergence evidence and a consistent description of the actual baseline implementations are needed to interpret the ranking.

The performance narrative overstates the evidence. The complete model trails M3D on ROUGE-L, METEOR, and GREEN, and its BLEU-4 advantage is only 0.002. It also trails the attribute-only variant on BLEU-4 and GREEN. The dismissal of CT2Rep’s substantially higher GREEN score as normal-case bias is unsupported by stratified analysis. No confidence intervals or repeated-run results establish the reliability of the modest improvements.

The central region-focused and clinical claims receive limited direct validation. There are no per-region results, lesion-size or localization measurements, segmentation-quality analyses, or tests of sensitivity to erroneous masks. Selecting each organ’s maximum-area slice does not necessarily retain its abnormal findings, particularly after reducing volumes to 32 slices. Aggregate report metrics and one qualitative example do not establish comprehensive regional coverage, reduced hallucinations, or the claimed interpretability.

The ablations do not fully isolate the proposed mechanisms. R2 versus uniform LITA sampling is evaluated without the other two components, leaving its contribution in the complete system unclear. There is no control separating the benefit of structured regional report supervision from architectural changes, and no attribute-only prompting baseline to measure how much performance comes directly from the segmentation-derived text.

Efficiency and reproducibility claims remain incomplete. Token-count reduction is demonstrated, but end-to-end latency, memory, and segmentation overhead are not measured. The exact mapping of 197 anatomical regions into six groups and the lesion-mask generation procedure are insufficiently specified. The abstract states that code is publicly available, but the supplied manuscript contains no repository link. Together with the methodological and evaluation concerns above, these gaps favor rejection despite the promising application.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision application: generating anatomically organized reports from volumetric CT. Combining global slice coverage, regional visual features, and quantitative anatomical attributes is clinically motivated and forms a coherent framework.

R2 pooling offers a simple, practical adaptation of slow–fast tokenization: selecting representative slices by anatomical mask area while retaining pooled tokens from every input slice. Reducing the visual sequence from D×T to D+T tokens is an appealing design.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence for the combined framework. It achieves the highest clinical-label F1 among the evaluated baselines (0.450 versus 0.435 for M3D), and component ablations improve F1 from 0.405 with R2 alone to 0.450 with the full model.

The evaluation uses an established dataset and its official patient split, multiple linguistic and clinical metrics, and component ablations. The supplement supplies useful training settings, and the manuscript acknowledges the prior methods underlying its components.
weaknesses: The quantitative attribute extractor has a consequential physical-units problem as documented. Supplementary Fig. 4 computes volume by summing mask voxels and diameter from bounding-box extents in voxel coordinates, while Fig. 5 labels these quantities as mL and mm. No voxel-spacing multiplication or volume-unit conversion is shown. Bounding-box extent is also only an approximate lesion diameter. Since quantitative attributes are a central contribution, the paper needs physically correct definitions and validation of measurement accuracy; omitted implementation details would need clarification.

The comparisons do not adequately establish the contribution relative to the closest prior work. Reg2RG already uses segmentation-derived regional CT features but is discussed without being evaluated. The components substantially adapt LITA, MAIRA-SEG/Osprey, and prior attribute-to-text methods, making this comparison particularly important. Moreover, all experiments are capped at 48 hours, and the authors explicitly acknowledge insufficient training of CT2Rep. This supports a resource-constrained comparison rather than an unqualified state-of-the-art claim. The supplement's assertion that all baselines use LLaMA3-8B also conflicts with the main text's CT2Rep description.

The results support narrower claims than the manuscript makes. The full model trails M3D on ROUGE-L, METEOR, and GREEN, and trails CT2Rep substantially on GREEN (0.278 versus 0.374). The explanation that CT2Rep's GREEN result is biased by normal-case overfitting is not supported by stratified analysis. The full model also does not consistently outperform its ablations. Its small advantage over M3D in BLEU-4 and clinical-label F1 is reported without uncertainty estimates.

Clinical reliability and regional grounding remain insufficiently validated. There is no per-region or per-abnormality breakdown, quantitative localization evaluation, or expert assessment supporting the claims of reduced hallucination and improved interpretability. The single qualitative example cannot establish these properties. Because the same pseudo-masks drive slice selection, regional tokens, and textual measurements, segmentation errors could affect all three pathways, yet mask quality and robustness to missing or inaccurate masks are not evaluated.

Several practical claims remain under-specified. Token reduction is not accompanied by end-to-end latency or memory measurements including segmentation and regional report generation. Reproduction would also benefit from explicit handling of empty masks, the anatomical-to-six-region mapping, lesion-mask generation settings, and an accessible code link; the manuscript states that code is public but provides no repository URL.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer vision problem: preserving localized diagnostic evidence when compressing 3D CT scans for report generation. The combination of anatomy-guided tokenization, volumetric mask pooling, and explicit lesion attributes is coherent and clinically motivated.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across 1,551 internal and 500 external cases. MedRegion-CT leads all reported internal metrics, including GREEN of 0.4555 versus 0.4013 for the strongest baseline, and achieves the highest external clinical-metric point estimates. Fine-tuning all five baselines on the structured training dataset improves comparison fairness.

The blinded reader study offers useful evidence beyond automated evaluation: one senior radiology resident scores the method 6.98 versus 4.44 for the strongest baseline on 50 external cases. Although limited in scale, this supports the practical relevance of the improvements.

The supplementary material strengthens the submission through region-level evaluation, size-stratified nodule analysis, segmentation perturbation experiments, and training details. Reporting the substantial small-nodule failure is valuable transparency.
weaknesses: The algorithmic advance over closely related region-guided methods is insufficiently established. Reg2RG is explicitly described as combining CT anatomical masks, local features, and global context, yet is absent from the experimental comparisons. The mask extractor adapts Osprey, while attribute prompting builds on established approaches. A direct comparison with Reg2RG and a simple baseline using the same lesion prompts would help establish the value of the proposed integration.

The ablations provide weak evidence for the necessity of all three components. In Table 2, adding Mask to R+Attr changes internal GREEN only from 0.4010 to 0.4025 and GPT-CA from 0.3807 to 0.3839. R alone also does not consistently outperform conventional SlowFast: its internal GPT-CA is lower, and external GPT-CA is nearly identical. Paired uncertainty estimates and comparisons using the same encoder and token budget are needed to support the stronger architectural claims.

Segmentation errors create a consequential failure mode for the claimed fine-grained diagnostic reliability. Table S3 reports small-nodule detection of 0.1270, compared with 0.2857–0.3651 for baselines. Algorithm 1 converts an empty predicted mask into the categorical statement 'No lesion is present,' potentially reinforcing false negatives. The analysis attributes failures to the upstream segmentor but does not test whether this prompting choice amplifies them. Size-category thresholds, the unusual ≤5 mm³ definition, and independent validation of the TotalSegmentator/RadBERT-based detection evaluation also require clarification.

The quantitative lesion attributes are not validated as measurements. Keeping only the largest connected component per anatomical region discards additional lesions, and the maximum axis-aligned bounding-box extent is not generally equivalent to a clinical lesion diameter. Intersecting lesions with anatomical masks can also truncate their extent. Without measurement-error or multiple-lesion evaluation, claims of precise quantitative clinical reporting remain insufficiently supported.

The structured benchmark lacks a reported clinical fidelity audit of the LLM-based report transformation. Abbreviation expansion, anatomical merging, and removal of longitudinal information can alter clinically meaningful content. Since both training targets and evaluation references undergo this process, sampled expert verification is important. The reader study is encouraging but uses one reader and a broad subjective score; it does not separately quantify critical omissions, hallucinations, or measurement accuracy.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete. The manuscript does not specify the TotalSegmentator version and lesion-task configurations, mask-perturbation procedure, full report-transformation prompts, or sufficiently precise slow-path sampling and sequence-overflow handling. No token-count distribution, end-to-end latency, or memory comparison supports the efficiency claims. The abstract also leaves the claimed public-code URL blank. These gaps matter for reproducing a pipeline whose behavior depends heavily on preprocessing and external models.

strengths: The framework addresses an important computer vision problem: preserving localized anatomical and pathological information when compressing 3D CT scans for report generation. Combining regional visual features with explicit lesion measurements is clinically motivated and technically plausible.

Table 1 provides meaningful evidence of effectiveness. On 1,551 internal test scans, the method leads all five baselines across the reported metrics, including GREEN of 0.4555 versus 0.4013 for the strongest baseline. Baselines were fine-tuned on the same structured dataset, and bootstrap confidence intervals are reported.

Evaluation extends beyond the internal dataset to 500 external cases. The method achieves the highest external clinical metric point estimates, although it does not lead the lexical metrics. A blinded, single-reader evaluation of 50 cases also favors the method substantially: 6.98 versus 4.44 for the strongest baseline.

The supplementary material provides useful training details, component ablations, regional results, segmentation perturbation experiments, and lesion-size analysis. Explicitly reporting poor small-nodule performance is valuable transparency.
weaknesses: The algorithmic contribution is insufficiently distinguished from closely related work. No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The method combines SlowFast-style tokenization, Osprey-derived mask pooling, and deterministic measurement prompts. Reg2RG is explicitly described as already combining anatomical CT masks with local and global features, yet it is absent from the experiments. A direct comparison and a clearer account of the technical advance over this particularly relevant predecessor are needed.

The ablations do not convincingly establish the importance of every proposed innovation. In Table 2, adding Mask to R+Attr changes internal GREEN only from 0.4010 to 0.4025 and GPT-CA from 0.3807 to 0.3839; paired uncertainty for these differences is not reported. The standalone regional tokenizer is also mixed against conventional SlowFast: internal GPT-CA is lower, while external GPT-CA is nearly identical. Experiments granting conventional tokenizers the same attribute prompts and mask features would better isolate the proposed tokenization benefit.

The lesion-prompt construction introduces clinically consequential failure modes. Algorithm 1 converts an empty predicted mask into the categorical statement that no lesion is present, conflating segmentation failure with actual absence. It also retains only the largest connected component per anatomical region, discarding additional lesions. Table S3 reports small-nodule detection of 0.1270, versus 0.2857–0.3651 for every baseline. This substantial regression directly qualifies the claims of reliable fine-grained reporting; attributing it to the upstream segmentor does not resolve the resulting system limitation.

The structured benchmark lacks demonstrated reference fidelity. Section 3.4 uses an LLM pipeline to cleanse, remove temporal information, and merge findings in both training and evaluation reports, but reports no expert audit of whether clinically important findings, negation, and uncertainty survive this transformation. The reader study helps, but its single-reader, report-referenced design does not establish the correctness of the transformed benchmark against the images. Thus, agreement with these references cannot fully substantiate the broad clinical reliability claims.

Quantitative lesion accuracy is asserted without direct measurement validation. The reported diameter is the largest axis-aligned bounding-box extent, whose agreement with clinically used measurements is not evaluated. There are no localization, volume, or diameter error results against expert annotations. The size-stratified analysis also omits most bin boundaries and uses an unclear small-lesion threshold of 5 mm³, limiting interpretation of this important experiment.

Efficiency and reproducibility remain incompletely supported. The manuscript claims substantial token compression but provides no token-count distribution, memory measurements, or end-to-end runtime including segmentation. Equation 3 does not fully specify depth sampling and spatial mask-to-token indexing. Segmentation versions/tasks, mask perturbation procedures, and benchmark-construction prompts are insufficiently detailed, and the abstract's public-code statement has no link. These gaps make the claimed efficiency and benchmark difficult to independently verify.

strengths: The framework addresses an important computer-vision application through a coherent combination of anatomy-guided tokenization, multi-layer regional pooling, and explicit lesion attributes. The relationship between these components and structured CT reporting is clearly motivated.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence: the method leads all six internal metrics across 1,551 scans, including GREEN of 0.4555 versus 0.4013 for the strongest baseline. All comparison models are fine-tuned on the structured training dataset.

Evaluation includes 500 external cases without additional training. The method achieves the highest external clinical-metric point estimates, and a blinded reader study provides complementary evidence, with a mean score of 6.98 versus 4.44 for the strongest comparator.

The supplementary material meaningfully examines regional performance, lesion size, and segmentation perturbations. Reporting the small-nodule failure mode is valuable, and training hyperparameters and bootstrap confidence intervals improve experimental transparency.
weaknesses: The algorithmic contribution is insufficiently isolated from existing methods and additional segmentation-derived information. Reg2RG, explicitly discussed as combining CT anatomical masks with local and global features, is absent from the comparisons. Table 2 also lacks conventional tokenization supplied with the same attribute and mask inputs. Consequently, the benefits of the proposed tokenizer versus access to explicit lesion information remain uncertain.

The clinical reliability claims exceed the lesion-level evidence. Table S3 reports small-nodule detection of 0.1270, compared with 0.2857–0.3651 for every baseline. Algorithm 1 converts an empty predicted mask into an explicit statement that no lesion is present, potentially reinforcing segmentation false negatives. Attributing failures to the upstream segmentor does not resolve this limitation of the complete system.

The lesion-attribute procedure has clinically consequential simplifications that are not validated. Keeping only the largest connected component per anatomical region discards additional lesions, while the largest axis-aligned bounding-box extent is only a proxy for lesion diameter. No measurement-error analysis establishes whether these textual attributes improve quantitative reporting accuracy.

The benchmark depends on LLM-based rewriting of both training and evaluation reports, including removal of longitudinal comparisons, but no expert audit quantifies retained findings, omissions, or introduced errors. The single-reader, 50-case study is useful preliminary evidence, yet its subjective report-reference scoring does not independently validate the benchmark or establish image-grounded diagnostic accuracy.

Some component claims are stronger than the ablations support. Adding Mask to R+Attr changes internal GREEN only from 0.4010 to 0.4025 and GPT-CA from 0.3807 to 0.3839. Paired uncertainty estimates or repeated runs are needed to establish these small gains; the available results do not demonstrate that all three modules are necessary.

Reproducibility and efficiency remain incompletely documented. Equation 3 does not clearly specify depth subsampling or management of variable token counts within the 8,192-token context. Token-count distributions, end-to-end runtime including segmentation, exact segmentation configurations, and mask-perturbation parameters are missing. The promised code URL is also absent. Overall, the promising empirical gains make this a close decision, but the attribution and clinical-validation concerns favor borderline rejection.
